title: Penalty Cards
summary: Stack penalties with an accumulator variable: a 2 adds two cards, a 3 adds three, a Joker adds five, and the next player either counters (same-rank penalty or an Ace) or picks up the lot.

lessons.title: The Accumulator Pattern for Penalties
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# The Accumulator Pattern

An **accumulator** is a variable that grows (or shrinks) across iterations or events. In Kadi the penalty stack is the canonical accumulator: each penalty card adds its value, and the next player must either counter or pick up the running total.

```gdscript
var penalty_stack: int = 0

func apply_penalty_card(card: CardData) -> void:
    match card.rank:
        CardTypes.Ranks.TWO:
            penalty_stack += 2
        CardTypes.Ranks.THREE:
            penalty_stack += 3
        CardTypes.Ranks.JOKER:
            penalty_stack += 5
        _:
            pick_up(penalty_stack)
            penalty_stack = 0

func pick_up(count: int) -> void:
    for _ in range(count):
        if GameState.deck.size() > 0:
            GameState.hands[GameState.current_player].append(
                GameState.deck.pop_back())
```

`+=` is compound assignment — shorthand for `penalty_stack = penalty_stack + 2`. Use it for any variable that changes by a delta.

The accumulator persists across turns because it lives on the TurnManager (a Node in the scene tree, not a local). When a player picks up, the accumulator **resets to 0** — that reset is the rule, not an optimisation.

> [!WHY]
> Penalties are the heart of Kadi's tension. By making `penalty_stack` an explicit, observable variable rather than recomputing it from history, every UI element (a stack counter, an animation, an AI's threat assessment) can read it directly via a signal. The accumulator turns "what is the current threat?" into an O(1) field read, not a scan of the discard pile.

Always reset accumulators at the documented rule boundary — here, when a player picks up — or the stack leaks into the next round.

practicePrompt.instructions: Add a `total_cards_picked_up: int` accumulator and increment it by `count` inside `pick_up` so we can display lifetime stats.
practicePrompt.hint: Declare a new field and use `+=`.

choices: Adds 3 to penalty_stack (equivalent to penalty_stack = penalty_stack + 3)
quizQuestions.explanation: `+=` is compound assignment: it adds the right operand to the left variable and stores the result back.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why must the penalty stack be reset to 0 when a player picks up?
choices: Because the rule says the stack is cleared once picked up — otherwise the same penalty haunts the next round
quizQuestions.explanation: The Kadi rule is that picking up consumes the entire stack. Failing to reset leaks the penalty into subsequent turns, breaking the game balance.

lessons.title: Countering a Penalty
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Countering a Penalty

A penalty stack is not a sentence — the next player has ways out. In Kadi, when you face a live penalty you may **avoid picking up** by either playing another **penalty card of the same rank** (which forwards the whole stack to the *next* player) or playing an **Ace** (which cancels the pick-up; play then continues with the suit that was in force before the penalty). If you can do neither, you draw the full stack and it resets to zero.

```gdscript
func can_counter(card: CardData, top_penalty: CardData) -> bool:
    if top_penalty == null:
        return false
    if card.rank == CardTypes.Ranks.ACE:
        return true
    return card.rank == top_penalty.rank

func resolve_penalty(card: CardData) -> void:
    if not can_counter(card, GameState.top_penalty):
        pick_up(GameState.penalty_stack)
        GameState.penalty_stack = 0
        return
    if card.rank == CardTypes.Ranks.ACE:
        GameState.penalty_stack = 0  # Ace cancels the stack
        return
    GameState.penalty_stack += penalty_value(card.rank)  # same-rank forwards it on
```

Notice the **guard clauses**: each `return` handles one outcome and exits, so the happy path never nests three levels deep. Reading top to bottom, the function says: 'can't counter? pick up and stop. Ace? clear the stack and stop. Otherwise forward the penalty.'

An important subtlety from the rules: forwarding with a same-rank penalty only *moves* the obligation — it does not clear it — while an Ace *cancels* it outright. Modelling those two counters as separate branches keeps each rule honest.

> [!WHY]
> Early-return guard clauses turn a tangled `if/else` tree into a checklist. Each branch owns exactly one rule outcome and is independently testable, so when a designer asks 'what happens if I play an Ace on a 3?' you point at one line. Bundling all three outcomes into nested conditionals is how subtle penalty-leak bugs — the stack surviving when it should have cleared — sneak in.

Prefer 'handle-and-return' for each special case; leave the ordinary path unindented at the bottom.

codeSnippets.caption: Guard clauses resolve the three penalty responses: pick up, cancel with Ace, or forward.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write `is_ace_escape(card)` returning true when the card is an Ace, using a single guard-clause return. This is the counter that cancels a penalty outright.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func is_ace_escape(card: CardData) -> bool:
    return card.rank == CardTypes.Ranks.ACE

quizQuestions.prompt: A player facing a penalty plays a card of the SAME rank as the penalty card. What happens?
choices: The whole penalty stack is forwarded to the next player
quizQuestions.explanation: Playing a same-rank penalty does not cancel the penalty; it adds to and forwards the entire stack to the next player, who must then respond.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why express the three penalty responses as early-return guard clauses instead of nested if/else?
choices: Each outcome is handled and exited in one place, keeping the happy path flat and each rule independently testable
quizQuestions.explanation: Guard clauses give every special case its own exit, so the logic reads as a checklist and penalty-leak bugs are far harder to introduce.
